analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties and requires public payroll records on federal construction wage law.
analysis.headline: The bill to tighten enforcement of the federal prevailing wage law for construction workers was introduced in December 2007, sent to two House committees, referred to a subcommittee in February 2008, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act sets minimum 'prevailing' wages for workers on federal construction contracts. This bill would make sure contractors who violate those wage rules can be barred from winning federal contracts for three years, applying that penalty across all federal laws that require prevailing wages. It would also require every federal agency to release the certified payroll records from those contracts to the public, with Social Security numbers removed, so anyone could check whether workers were actually paid the required wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers on federally funded projects gain a stronger deterrent against wage violations, because a company that disregards its wage obligations can be barred from federal contracts for three years. The public also gains access to contractor payroll records, making it easier for workers, unions, and watchdogs to verify that prevailing wages were actually paid.

how_it_helps.text: It writes the Davis-Bacon debarment provision — a three-year ban on federal contracts for firms that disregarded their obligations to employees and subcontractors — into every federal law requiring prevailing wages, so the penalty applies consistently rather than depending on which statute a contract falls under.

It requires each federal agency to make the complete payroll records from Davis-Bacon-covered contracts available to the public, excluding Social Security numbers, letting anyone check whether workers were paid the required wages.

analysis.who_pays: Federal construction contractors and their related firms bear the cost: violations of wage obligations could now trigger a three-year ban from federal contracting, and their payroll records — including names and wages of workers — would become public information.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds disclosure obligations and a stricter debarment regime for federal contractors, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that three-year contract bans can be a blunt instrument for violations that vary widely in seriousness, potentially deterring some firms from bidding on federal work at all.
Publishing full payroll records, even without Social Security numbers, exposes workers' names and earnings to public view, which some would argue is a privacy trade-off for transparency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers on federal construction jobs, the bill's value is real but targeted: it hardens enforcement of wage rules that already exist and adds public verification of payroll compliance. The costs fall on contractors and are modest in scope — no new wages are mandated, only tougher consequences for not paying the ones already required. The bill never received committee action or a vote, so its design was never tested through amendment or debate.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and was sent to a subcommittee, and it died there when that Congress ended in January 2009 without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the Davis-Bacon Enforcement Act of 2007 in the House on December 19, 2007.
The bill was referred to two committees — Education and Labor and Oversight and Government Reform — splitting its jurisdiction from the start.

On February 5, 2008, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained; no committee vote, floor vote, or further action followed before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
The bill had six Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and no version ever passed either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal construction contractors are better off, since the three-year debarment penalty and public payroll disclosure never became law. Construction workers on federal contracts are no better off, because enforcement of existing wage rules stays as it was.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 19, 2007 to strengthen Davis-Bacon enforcement and require public payroll disclosure.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee and House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 19, 2007; neither committee acted on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 5, 2008 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no opposition is on the record; the bill's sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats, and it drew no Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would expose them to a three-year federal contracting ban for disregarding wage obligations and would make their payroll records public. Contractors that underpay workers benefit from the weaker enforcement that exists instead.

industries.industry: Construction workers and building trades unions
industries.note: Workers on prevailing-wage federal contracts would gain a concrete enforcement tool and public payroll records that make it easier to detect wage violations.
Contractors that already pay prevailing wages face little new burden, and public payroll records would level the playing field against competitors who shave wages to win bids.
